analysis.one_liner: Replaces private health insurance with a government-run plan offering free care to everyone in the U.S.
analysis.headline: A universal government health insurance bill with 93 House Democratic cosponsors never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote during the two years Democrats controlled the House.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a national health insurance program covering every person living in the United States, with no deductibles, copays, or coinsurance for medically necessary care — including doctor visits, hospital stays, prescriptions, dental, vision, hearing, mental health, and long-term care. Private insurers would be barred from selling coverage that duplicates these benefits, and hospitals would have to convert from for-profit to nonprofit status over 15 years. The program would be funded by redirecting existing federal health spending, raising income taxes on the top 5% of earners, a progressive payroll tax, and a small tax on stock and bond trades.
analysis.who_benefits: Every person living in the United States, insured or not: the program covers all medically necessary care with no cost-sharing, and patients keep free choice of any participating doctor or hospital. People who currently lose coverage when they change or lose jobs would carry their card anywhere in the country. Clerical and billing workers whose insurance-industry jobs are eliminated would get first priority in retraining and two years of unemployment benefits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: All U.S. residents, especially the uninsured

how_it_helps.text: All individuals residing in the United States and its territories would be covered, receiving a national health insurance card with no deductibles, copayments, or coinsurance on covered benefits.

Benefits would include the full scope of medical care: primary and preventive care, inpatient and outpatient care, emergency care, prescription drugs, long-term care, mental health and substance abuse treatment, dental, vision, hearing including hearing aids, and chiropractic services.
Patients would keep free choice of participating physicians, hospitals, and facilities, and benefits would be portable to any licensed clinician anywhere in the country.
Clerical, administrative, and billing personnel whose jobs are eliminated by reduced administration would get first priority in retraining and job placement and two years of unemployment benefits.

Financing would draw on existing federal health revenues, higher personal income taxes on the top 5% of earners, a progressive excise tax on payroll and self-employment income, and a small tax on stock and bond transactions, with savings from reduced paperwork and bulk drug purchasing.

analysis.who_pays: The top 5% of income earners would pay higher income taxes; workers and the self-employed would pay a progressive payroll tax; investors would pay a small tax on stock and bond transactions. For-profit hospitals and other investor-owned care facilities would have to convert to nonprofit status over 15 years — owners would be compensated for appraised property and equipment through Treasury bonds, but not for lost business profits. Private health insurers would lose the core of their business.
analysis.who_pays_short: Top earners, payroll taxpayers, private insurers

drawbacks.text: The bill would eliminate private health insurance as it exists today, making it unlawful for insurers to sell coverage duplicating program benefits — a massive disruption for an industry employing hundreds of thousands in administrative and billing roles, only partly cushioned by two years of unemployment benefits and retraining priority.

Investor-owned hospitals, nursing homes, and clinics could participate only by converting to nonprofit status over 15 years, funded through Treasury bond sales; owners would be paid for property and equipment but not for lost business profits, a major financial hit to for-profit care chains.

The financing relies on new broad-based taxes, including a payroll tax on workers and the self-employed and a transaction tax on stock and bond trades, and the bill leaves the exact rates to future appropriation rather than specifying them.

Hospitals and other institutions would be paid through annually negotiated global budgets rather than per-patient reimbursement, and drug prices would be set through an annual negotiation with a formulary that steers patients to generics — providers and drug makers would face tighter revenue constraints than today.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For most households, the trade is direct: new taxes replace premiums, deductibles, and copays, and coverage becomes universal and unconditional. The genuinely difficult costs fall on two groups — the insurance industry's administrative workforce, whose jobs are scheduled for elimination (mitigated but not erased by two years of benefits and retraining), and taxpayers, who would fund a 15-year buyout of for-profit care facilities through Treasury bonds. The bill's biggest practical weakness is that it fixes tax rates and global budgets only in general terms, leaving the hardest fiscal decisions to a future program director and Congress.

outcome.mechanism: After being referred to three House committees and then to their health subcommittees, the bill received no hearing, no markup, and no vote in the Democratic-controlled House, and it died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. John Conyers of Michigan introduced the bill on January 24, 2007, joined on introduction by dozens of original cosponsors including Reps. Kucinich, McDermott, Rangel, and George Miller.
The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Natural Resources Committees, and within days to the health subcommittees of Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means.
It attracted 93 cosponsors, every one of them a Democrat, in a House where Democrats held the majority after the 2006 elections.

No hearing, subcommittee vote, full committee markup, or floor vote ever took place; the action history ends with the 2007 subcommittee referrals, and the bill expired when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The private health insurance industry and for-profit hospital and care chains kept their place in the health system untouched. The tens of millions of Americans without coverage in 2007, and households facing premiums and cost-sharing, gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private insurers and for-profit care providers

for.name: Rep. John Conyers, Jr.
for.role: Sponsor, U.S. National Health Insurance Act
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 24, 2007 and recruited 93 cosponsors, all Democrats, over the two-year session.

for.name: 93 of 233 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill — the broadest recorded support for a single-payer bill to that point — but the cosponsor list alone produced no committee action.

for.name: Rep. Dennis Kucinich
for.role: Original cosponsor and leading single-payer advocate
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor at introduction and championed the bill publicly.

against.name: Rep. John Dingell
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the primary referral of the bill; under his chairmanship the committee held no hearing and took no action on it during the Congress.

against.name: Rep. Charles Rangel
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill himself, but his committee, which held jurisdiction over the bill's tax and Medicare provisions, took no action after referral to its Health Subcommittee.

against.name: Speaker Nancy Pelosi
against.what_they_did: The bill was never scheduled for House floor consideration during two years of Democratic majority control.

against.name: America's Health Insurance Plans (AHIP) and the health insurance industry
against.what_they_did: Campaigned against single-payer legislation, which would ban insurers from selling coverage duplicating the universal program and end the industry's core business.

sides.party_line_note: All 93 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican supported the bill; the deciding inaction, however, came from the Democratic majority's own committee chairs and leadership, who never moved it to a vote.

industries.note: The bill makes it unlawful for a private insurer to sell coverage duplicating the universal program's benefits, ending the industry's core business of covering medically necessary care; only supplementary coverage for non-medically-necessary services (like cosmetic surgery) would remain legal. Insurers' interests ran against the public's interest in universal, cost-sharing-free coverage.

For-profit hospitals, nursing homes, and clinics could participate only by converting to nonprofit status over 15 years, with owners compensated for appraised property and equipment but not for lost business profits. Their gain under the status quo ( profits from delivering care paid for largely by public programs) came at ordinary patients' expense.

Drug prices would be set through annual negotiation with a national formulary that steers prescribing toward generics, ending the pricing power drug companies hold over American patients today. Lower drug prices would run alongside patients' interest in affordable medicine.

Nonprofit providers would keep serving patients under guaranteed annual global budgets with simplified billing and no bad debt from the uninsured, but would face annual budget negotiations and limits on capital spending instead of fee-for-service revenue growth.

industries.industry: Health insurance administrative and billing workforce
industries.note: Clerical, administrative, and billing jobs at insurance companies and provider offices would be eliminated by reduced administration; the bill provides first-priority retraining and two years of unemployment benefits, acknowledging the jobs would not survive.
